title: 2018_PMC5945909_Parents_attitudes_towards_topical_fluoride_and_vaccines_for_chil
ehr_evidence: We assessed dental chart-based topical ﬂuoride refusal occurring in 2009 or 2010 and parent-reported vaccine refusal.
summary: A 1:1 matched case-control study of 361 parents of children from three Washington state dental clinics examining whether parental attitudes and Internet use regarding topical fluoride and vaccines overlap and correlate with child fluoride and vaccine refusal.
key_findings: Topical fluoride and vaccine refusal were modestly correlated (r = 0.23).
In adjusted full models, none of the fluoride-specific items were significantly associated with fluoride refusal; only non-fluoride toothpaste use remained significant (PR = 2.25, 95% CI 1.56-3.23).
For vaccine refusal, in the full model, perceived severity of preventable cavities (PR = 1.29, 95% CI 1.04-1.60), vaccine concern, and Internet use for vaccine information remained significant.
White respondents (vs. non-white) reported a 62% higher likelihood of vaccine refusal (PR = 1.62).
Income >$40,000-$60,000 (vs. >$60,000) was associated with 45% lower likelihood of fluoride refusal.
captured_features: Disapproval of dental x-rays, amalgam and composite fillings
Parent age, education, income, dental insurance; child sex, age, race/ethnicity; clinic site
study_design: Case-control study (matched 1:1 on fluoride status, clinic, age, gender) with survey-based cross-sectional analysis
population: 361 parents of children from three Washington state dental clinics; children seen for dental checkups in 2009-2010; mean child age 11.14 years (range 2.33-20.12); US setting
exposure_domain: Parental attitudes (safety concerns, perceived severity, Internet information-seeking) and vaccine/fluoride hesitancy
limitations: Vaccine refusal was self-reported while fluoride refusal was chart-based, introducing differential measurement.
Limited generalizability to three Washington state clinics all in fluoridated-water areas.
Did not account for parental dental/medical history and omitted domains of the Health Belief and Extended Parallel Process Models.
